name: Mastic / hard gum
lead: Mastic gum is a chewable resin obtained from the mastic tree (Pistacia lentiscus var. chia), cultivated mainly on the southern part of the Greek island of Chios, and it is also the base of several commercial chewing gums.[1][18] In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed, together with other firm or long-lasting gums such as the Turkish brand Falim and branded 'jawline' gums, as a way to give the jaw muscles resistance training in the hope of a more defined lower face.[10][11][12][22]

The mechanism proponents describe is simple: a stiffer, slower-softening gum makes the masseter and temporalis work harder for longer than ordinary supermarket gum, and a larger or stronger masseter is expected to change the look of the lower face over months of regular chewing. Forum users compare mastic against Falim and regular gum, swap routines and before-and-after impressions, and ask how long visible changes take.[10][22][23]

The resin itself has a long history in Mediterranean traditional medicine, particularly for digestive complaints, and has been examined in small clinical trials for stomach and duodenal conditions.[1][5][6][7] Those studies concern digestive and other health outcomes, not facial appearance. No published controlled study has tested whether chewing mastic or other hard gum changes jaw shape or facial definition in healthy adults; related research is limited to short-term measurements of masseter muscle stiffness and oxygen dynamics after chewing, and to epidemiological work on gum chewing and temporomandibular disorder.[2][3][4]

chain: Chew a dense, slow-softening gum for extended sessions
Masseter and temporalis work against more resistance than with soft gum
Proponents expect firmer, larger masticatory muscle and a more defined lower face
angle.text: Mastic and other hard gums are used as a food-based jaw workout: the muscles of mastication are loaded by chewing, and users hope that over time this adds muscle definition along the jaw. Published studies have measured short-term muscle responses to chewing, not changes in facial shape.

paras: Mastic is an aromatic resin that hardens into small pale tears after being exuded from incisions in the bark of the mastic tree.[1] When chewed it first stays brittle, then softens into an opaque white gum with a pine-like, slightly bitter flavour.[18] The name is thought to be related to the Greek verb for chewing, and in modern Hebrew the colloquial word for chewing gum is derived from it.[18]

The resin is chewed as a gum, used in liqueurs such as Mastika, in confectionery, ice cream and baking across the Mediterranean and Middle East, and in cosmetics, perfumery, incense and varnishes.[1][18] Mastic is also an ingredient in some dental varnishes, where it serves as the resin component.[26]

Harvesting on Chios runs from early July to early October. Growers clear the ground under each tree, then make several shallow incisions in the bark every few days; the exuded sap takes roughly two to three weeks to harden into droplets that are collected, washed and sorted.[18] As of 2024 there are twenty-four mastic villages on the island, and production is managed by a grower cooperative founded in 1938.[18] The name 'Masticha Chiou' is protected by an EU protected designation of origin, and the traditional cultivation know-how was added to UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list in 2014, according to one encyclopedic summary.[1][18] A small amount of mastic is also produced on the Cesme peninsula in Turkey, where a conservation foundation planted more than 3,000 saplings between 2008 and 2011.[18]

Chemical analyses identify a volatile fraction rich in alpha-pinene, myrcene and beta-caryophyllene, and a resin fraction made largely of triterpenoids.[1][14][15] A 1999 analysis of the essential oils of the gum, leaves and twigs identified 69 constituents.[14] This chemistry is the basis of most laboratory work on the resin's antimicrobial and antioxidant activity, and is unrelated to the mechanical idea behind jaw training.[14][15]

Chios mastic has been used as a traditional medicine for about 2,500 years. Wikipedia credits Hippocrates with the first mention of mastic tears, recommending it for digestive problems, colds and fresher breath, and notes that the resin was prized under the Byzantine and Ottoman empires; the Turkish name for Chios, Sakiz Adasi, means 'gum island'.[18] The mastic villages of southern Chios were built as walled, fortress-like settlements to protect the crop.[18] A forest fire in August 2012 destroyed part of the groves.[18]

Mastic's role as a modern chewing gum was boosted by commercial products. Grokipedia names the Turkish brand Falim, launched in the 1980s, as a mastic-flavoured gum that helped popularize the resin; Falim became the cheaper, widely available option that forum users set against pure Chios mastic.[1][22]

The jaw-training use appears to be a later, online development. A Hacker News submission from December 2020 linked to a page titled 'Health Benefits of Mastic Gum (and How It Sharpens Your Jawline)' on a site that appears to sell jawline gum; it drew one comment, unrelated to jaw effects.[20] On looksmax.org, threads on the topic include one asking how long it takes to get serious jawline gains from chewing mastic, one asking whether Falim thickens bone or only enlarges the masseter, and a long-running chewing megathread.[11][23][24] Branded hard gums marketed explicitly for the jaw have followed, including one the community discussed in 2023.[12]

In forum discussion, hard gum is presented as a food-based alternative to dedicated jaw exercisers. The idea is that sustained, forceful chewing loads the masseter and temporalis muscles, which proponents hope will thicken the muscle and sharpen the jaw or lower face. Threads on looksmax.org compare mastic with regular gum and gather chewing advice in a long-running megathread.[10][11]

Users describe pure Chios mastic as harder than Falim, which one poster called surprisingly soft and similar to ordinary gum; that poster said they chewed Falim first as a warm-up and then Chios mastic until the jaw felt sore.[21] Another thread debates which of the two is better, with one reply arguing for mastic partly because of its reported digestive benefits, including activity against Helicobacter pylori.[22] A further thread asks about cheaper alternatives to mastic, reflecting its price relative to supermarket gum.[25]

Brand-name gums marketed for the jaw have appeared in forum threads in which users ask about others' experiences.[12] Posters also ask how long mastic must be chewed before changes show, and how it compares with other chewing routines in the megathread.[11][23]

sections.h: How it is meant to work
paras: The masseter is the main elevator of the jaw and the muscle most associated with the angle and width of the lower face. The proposal is that, as with other skeletal muscle, repeated loading could raise its strength and size, and that harder gum raises the load. Forum members also ask whether chewing can thicken bone, not just muscle.[24]

Published research has addressed muscle response rather than appearance. In a within-subject study of 40 healthy adults aged about 19 to 61, shear wave elastography measured masseter stiffness at baseline, after ten minutes of chewing gum at roughly 1.5 chews per second, and after ten minutes of rest. Median masseter stiffness rose from about 11.4 to 12.5 kilopascals after chewing and fell to about 11.8 after rest; temporalis stiffness changed much less.[2] A 2024 report examined how a programme of gum-chewing training affected masseter muscle oxygen dynamics.[3] Neither study measured facial shape.

No randomized or controlled trial has examined mastic or hard gum for jawline definition, masseter size or facial contour in healthy adults. The shear wave study above was small, short-term, limited to a single chewing session in healthy volunteers who did not grind or clench, and used a gum that was not specified as mastic; the authors listed these as limitations.[2]

Chewing gum increases masticatory muscle activity, and researchers distinguish this from muscle hypertrophy or changes in bone contour; the published work above does not address whether the former leads to the latter.[2][3] Users on looksmax.org report their own impressions in threads, but these are self-reports without measurements.[11][23]

A 2014 study examined the association between temporomandibular disorder (TMD) and gum chewing.[4] Jaw clinicians commonly list habitual or prolonged chewing among behaviours to review in people with jaw-joint or muscle pain, and users on looksmax.org have themselves raised temporomandibular joint concerns in chewing discussions.[4][11]

One looksmax.org poster reported noticing gum recession after chewing hard Chios mastic and suggested that the gum had slipped against the gumline; the poster urged care to chew with the teeth only, and other users argued the chewing itself was not the cause.[21] This is an individual report and has not been studied.

Mastic is an Anacardiaceae resin, and Grokipedia notes that people sensitive to other plants of that family can react with allergic contact dermatitis.[1] A study screened 288 sera for IgG and IgE antibodies to a panel of gums, including mastic gum, and noted that gums have a history of sensitivity reactions.[13] Healthline lists headache, upset stomach and dizziness as possible effects and advises avoiding mastic during pregnancy and breastfeeding.[19] The European Medicines Agency advises against use in children and during pregnancy and breastfeeding because of insufficient data, according to Wikipedia.[18]

Hard or sticky gum may also affect dental restorations. Larger masseters would be expected to broaden rather than narrow the lower face, a point raised in forum discussion of jaw training generally.[11]

sections.h: Medical and traditional uses of mastic
paras: Outside appearance, mastic gum has been studied for digestive complaints. A 1984 double-blind trial compared mastic with placebo in duodenal ulcer, and a 2010 randomized, double-blind trial tested Chios mastic gum in functional dyspepsia.[5][6] A 2020 review summarizes traditional uses, phytochemistry and pharmacology,[7] and laboratory work has examined activity against Helicobacter pylori, oxidation of LDL and colon cancer cells.[8][9] Healthline summarises small studies on H. pylori clearance, Crohn's disease symptoms, cholesterol and cavity-associated bacteria, noting that most are small or preliminary.[19] A 2025 randomized trial examined Chios mastic toothpaste for halitosis in orthodontic patients,[27] a 2024 review discusses antidiabetic properties of the plant,[16] and a 2026 randomized trial (HYPER-MASTIC) evaluated Chios mastic supplementation in well-controlled hypertension.[17] These results relate to mastic as a supplement or medicine and not to the mechanical effects of chewing.[5][6][7]

Wikipedia reports that in 2016 the European Medicines Agency concluded that the available clinical studies were too small to support 'well-established use' of mastic, while still recognising powdered mastic as a traditional herbal medicinal product for mild dyspepsia and for minor skin inflammation and wounds; Grokipedia dates the dyspepsia recognition to 2015.[1][18] Grokipedia also reports that the US FDA lists mastic as generally recognized as safe as a food flavouring.[1] Healthline notes that dietary supplements are not regulated by the FDA in the way medicines are.[19]

No studies found on mastic or hard gum for jaw or facial appearance. Related human research is limited to a ten-minute chewing study of masseter stiffness in 40 healthy adults,[2] a report on masseter oxygen dynamics after gum chewing training,[3] and an epidemiological study of temporomandibular disorder and gum chewing.[4] Separate trials of mastic in duodenal ulcer, functional dyspepsia and hypertension concern digestive and cardiovascular outcomes.[5][6][17]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, hard gum and mastic appear in chewing threads where users compare gums, discuss routines and ask about branded jawline products.[10][11][12][22][23]

claims.claim: Mastic is a harder, longer-lasting chew than regular gum, so it trains the masseter better
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread is devoted to comparing mastic with regular gum for chewing, and a poster comparing Chios mastic with Falim describes the Chios gum as much harder and Falim as close to ordinary gum.[10][21]
claims.experts: No published study compares mastic with regular gum for muscle training. Short-term studies show masseter stiffness rises after chewing gum, without comparing gum types.[2]

claims.claim: Chewing hard gum can build a more defined jawline
claims.believers: The chewing megathread on looksmax.org collects discussion of chewing as a jaw-training practice, and other threads ask how long serious jawline gains take.[11][23]
claims.experts: No controlled study has measured jaw shape after hard-gum chewing. Researchers have measured only acute muscle stiffness and oxygen dynamics.[2][3]

claims.claim: Mastic or Falim gum can thicken the jaw bone as well as the masseter
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread asks whether Falim chewing only enlarges the masseter or also thickens bone, reflecting a belief that chewing can reshape the skeleton.[24]
claims.experts: No published study has measured jaw-bone changes from gum chewing; the available work measured muscle stiffness and oxygen dynamics.[2][3]

claims.claim: Branded jawline gums offer an advantage over supermarket gum
claims.believers: Users ask in a dedicated thread whether others have tried a new hard chewing gum, reflecting interest in the product's firmness.[12]
claims.experts: No independent trial of such products has been published.

claims.claim: Mastic is the better choice over Falim because it also has health benefits
claims.believers: One poster in a mastic-versus-Falim thread argues that mastic is preferable because studies report activity against H. pylori and anti-inflammatory properties, while both gums work for the masseter.[22]
claims.experts: Small trials in duodenal ulcer and functional dyspepsia exist and laboratory work shows activity against H. pylori; the European Medicines Agency judged the clinical studies too small for well-established use.[5][6][8][18]

claims.claim: Careless chewing of hard mastic can cause gum recession
claims.believers: A poster reports gum recession after hard Chios mastic slipped against the gumline and advises chewing with the teeth only, while another user says hard chewing done incorrectly can recede gums, as hard brushing can.[21]
claims.experts: No published study has examined mastic chewing and gum recession; dental clinicians generally review heavy habitual chewing in people with jaw or tooth problems.[4]

claims.claim: Heavy chewing can strain the jaw joint
claims.believers: Forum users themselves raise temporomandibular joint worries in chewing discussions.[11]
claims.experts: A 2014 study examined the association between temporomandibular disorder and gum chewing.[4]

claims.claim: Bigger masseters from chewing may widen rather than sharpen the lower face
claims.believers: Some forum members note that jaw-muscle growth adds width at the angle of the jaw and discuss whether that suits their face shape.[11]
claims.experts: No published study has measured facial width after chewing programmes; the stiffness study did not assess shape.[2]
